comparator.name: Theology
comparator.route: Systematic Theology with Biblical Greek and Hebrew
comparator.sourceNotes: This example combines the Systematic Theology track with biblical Greek, Hebrew and exegesis. Students can also choose a route without biblical languages. The degree includes a 30 EC minor and a 15 EC final research project.
components: Theology, Aesthetics and Culture A: Introduction
Theology, Aesthetics and Culture B: Research

routeSelection.route: Systematic Theology with Biblical Greek and Hebrew
routeSelection.basis: Four equally weighted tracks are available for the generic degree. Systematic Theology is first in the adopted regulations. The example uses the biblical-language route in the main curriculum table. These choices are independent of UCR fit.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Christian thought, systematic theology, worldview and questions of meaning
Historical, biblical and practical theology; religious texts; theology, aesthetics and culture
Greek, Hebrew, source-language exegesis and an independent theology final project
Religion, interreligious encounter, media and public life
Academic, philosophical, historical and interpretive inquiry
adjacent: Practical theology, ministry and spiritual care
questions: How do worldviews, texts and cultural traditions shape ideas of meaning, identity and the good life?
How do religious traditions interact with institutions, rights, conflict and contemporary public life?

trace: Develops academic inquiry, reflective learning and writing.
Examines empire, legitimacy, cultural authority and historical institutions.
Develops historical research design, critical source use and evidence-based writing.
Studies human rights, their justifications and freedom of religion.
Examines arguments about God, ethical theories, identity and meaning in life.
Examines divine command, moral reasoning, care and questions of meaning.
Examines accounts of mind and personal identity, including Buddhist non-self.
Examines political authority, justice and ideas of legitimate rule.
Examines conflict, historical grievances, reconciliation and the role of arts and religion.
Studies social structures, socialization, identity, belonging and othering.
Develops qualitative research, interviews, observation and documentary methods.
Examines civil society, public spheres, trust and solidarity.
Examines social influence, attitudes, group identity and prejudice.
Studies radicalization and resilience, including belonging, peer influence and counter-narratives.
Develops reasoning and audience-aware argument through rhetoric.
Introduces interpretation and historical context for Western art, including late-medieval and Renaissance works.
Uses material culture and archaeology to examine ancient social practices and identities.
Examines West African arts and the relationship between visual forms, religion and authority.
Examines Renaissance art across Europe and the Mediterranean, including connections with Islamic courts.
Examines modern visual culture, artistic movements, museums and reception.
Develops historical and methodological inquiry into aesthetics and the interpretation of images.
Examines literary traditions, ethical questions, narrative and identity through close reading.
Examines creation myths, religious motifs, narrative authority and cultural reception.
Examines media representations, racial exclusion and counternarratives.

alternatives.label: Worldviews, Cultural Traditions and Public Life
alternatives.concept: Explore how people give meaning to life and how worldviews shape culture and public life. Study philosophical arguments about belief and ethics, interpret myths and art, and use history and social science to investigate identity, rights and conflict.
alternatives.labelReason: The plan connects belief and moral philosophy, cultural interpretation and public life through evidence from several disciplines.
progression: Introductory art history, philosophy and sociology support later heritage, ethics and public culture study. Historical study precedes the advanced historical research course.

candidates.label: Biblical Languages and Exegesis
candidates.assessment: The Utrecht evidence independently confirms biblical studies, Greek, Hebrew and exegesis. Current UCR courses offer contextual, visual and literary methods but no sequence in biblical languages or scriptural interpretation. The detailed antiquity topics inherited from Groningen are not used to establish Utrecht requirements.

candidates.label: Practical Theology and Ministry Preparation
candidates.assessment: The current Utrecht target includes practical theology and a route preparing for the ministry master. UCR’s social science, psychology and communication courses do not supply practical theology, supervised pastoral practice or spiritual formation.

candidates.label: Groningen Theology Trajectory
candidates.assessment: The registry row describes a different offering. It is explicitly disposed of without generating UCR content for the Utrecht target.

selection.assessment: One UCR plan supports sustained inquiry into worldviews, cultural traditions and their public role. A biblical-language or pastoral route would require specialist coursework and practice beyond the UCR course offering.

blocks: PThU studies the history of Christian theology. UCR uses historical and cultural methods to study institutions and traditions.
PThU students engage with a recent theological publication.
PThU includes focused study of Judaism and Islam. UCR examines related traditions through selected cultural and historical cases.
PThU introduces Christian doctrine and theological ethics. UCR explores belief and moral reasoning through philosophy.
PThU studies the Reformation and its role in Protestant history.
PThU examines theological practice in settings such as churches and care.
PThU links theology and aesthetics. UCR studies visual culture and interpretation through art history.
PThU introduces academic study of the Bible. UCR develops broader literary and historical methods.
PThU develops research at the intersection of theology, aesthetics and culture.
PThU studies the foundations of scholarly inquiry in its theology curriculum.

notes.text: PThU studies theology in the Protestant Christian tradition. The UCR plan explores belief, meaning and the public role of religion through philosophy, history, the arts and social science.

Theology, biblical exegesis and supervised pastoral practice require dedicated study. PThU also offers a route in which students replace the language and exegesis courses with other theology courses and interreligious practice.

audience.programmeDescription: This Dutch-taught bachelor studies Christian theology, faith, meaning and religious practice in the Protestant tradition.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The PThU example shows Systematic Theology with biblical languages. The UCR plan explores worldviews through philosophy, cultural history and public life.
